logos.r11-01: The user's own build, drawn properly: two opposed bowls as one S, held in a rounded square. Matching round caps and joins throughout, counters opened so the letter still reads small.
logos.r11-02: Same S, but the container turns circular and the bowls thicken until the mark is mostly ink. The frame stops being a box and starts being a seal.
logos.r11-03: The S stops being a line and becomes mass. Two solid bowls meet on a shared diagonal seam, navy above and teal below — bolder by weight of ink, not by stroke width.
logos.r11-04: The S caught mid-join: the two halves have pulled apart and the break sits right on the spine. Still unmistakably the letter, but held one moment before it closes.
logos.r11-05: The container becomes the figure: a solid navy tile with the S cut clean out of it, teal showing through the hole. Nothing is outlined at all.
logos.r11-06: Real letterform stress: the upper bowl is smaller and lighter, the lower one wider and heavier, the way a typeface actually draws an S. The unevenness is regular enough to read as drawn, not as a slip.
logos.r11-07: Two heavy brackets face off and lock. Read once it is a pair of clasps in register; read twice and the S is sitting in the space they leave.
logos.r11-08: One unbroken ribbon, drawn in a single sweep, changing colour exactly where it crosses itself. Two things becoming one — the sync idea told as a handoff instead of an overlap.
logos.r11-09: The S flattened into three heavy slabs, stepped like a staircase. Almost nothing is curved, and it still reads as the letter at sixteen pixels.
logos.r11-10: The frame itself turns into the letter. Two opposite corners of the rounded square are cut open and swept inward, so the container and the S are the same single stroke.
